note: Per-match tactical breakdowns. Fields under `grounded` come from FotMob's match data and are never written by the LLM. Fields under `explained` are model commentary constrained to that data. `conceptsTaught` drives the lesson curriculum so it ramps instead of repeating.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal scored early — Ezri Konsa headed in from a Viktor Gyökeres assist in the 7th minute — and from then on Everton barely got out of their own half. Arsenal kept the ball more (58%), had 20 shots to Everton's 8, and won 12 corners to Everton's 3. Gabriel added a second on 68 minutes from a Ben White delivery, and 2-0 was a fair reflection of a game Arsenal controlled without ever needing to be frantic.
explained.opponentPlan: David Moyes set Everton up in a matching 4-2-3-1, but the numbers show they were not using it to compete for the ball — they were using it to deny space. Everton made more tackles (17 v 14) and more interceptions (8 v 4) than Arsenal, which is what happens when you spend the match defending your own box rather than dictating play: your defensive actions pile up because the ball keeps arriving. Arsenal answered it the only way you can answer a compact, matched-up defence — by going wide and going again. 266 passes in the opposition half, 47 touches in Everton's box and 12 corners is the signature of a team patiently circulating the ball until a gap or a set-piece appears, and both goals came from exactly that route, with defenders Konsa and Gabriel on the end of them.
explained.keyMoment: Konsa's goal on 7 minutes, assisted by Gyökeres, is the moment that defines the shape of the whole match. Once Arsenal led that early, Everton had to come out at some point, but never really did — and Arsenal were free to settle into the slow, wide, corner-generating rhythm that produced 20 shots, 12 of them inside the box. Gabriel's header on 68 from Ben White's delivery was the same pattern paying out a second time: the pressure didn't spike, it just accumulated.
explained.nerdCorner: The interesting tension is between the shot count and the on-target count: 20 shots producing only 4 on target, yet xGOT (2.26) came in above xG (1.96). Those two things point in opposite directions. The first says Arsenal were taking a lot of low-value, blocked or speculative attempts against a packed box — exactly what 12 corners and a deep Everton block will generate. The second says that the shots which did get through were struck or headed into good spots, so the post-shot quality was higher than the pre-shot quality. Read together, the profile is a team whose volume is inflated by dead-ball situations but whose actual finishing in this match was clean. Also worth sitting with: Everton registered 2 big chances to Arsenal's 3 and forced 3 saves from Raya. The 2-0 looks comfortable, and the territory genuinely was, but Everton were never more than one moment from making it awkward — which is usually what a mid-block is designed to buy you.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper this is a 4-2-3-1, but Arsenal rarely keep that shape with the ball. One full-back — in this line-up Myles Lewis-Skelly — typically steps inside next to Declan Rice or Mikel Merino, which leaves three defenders behind the ball and two midfielders in front of them, while the front five (Noni Madueke, Martin Ødegaard, Eberechi Eze, Viktor Gyökeres and the advanced full-back) stretch across the width of the final third. When Arsenal lose the ball, that full-back drops back out to the touchline and the front four fold back into a flat bank, so the team looks like a conventional back four again.

lesson.explain: Set-piece xG is simply the share of your chance quality that comes from corners and free-kicks rather than from open play. It matters because set-pieces are the one phase where a well-drilled team can manufacture chances against an opponent who has otherwise shut the game down — you don't need to break them open, you just need the ball in the air. Arsenal won 12 corners to Everton's 3 here, and both goals were scored by centre-backs, Konsa on 7 and Gabriel on 68 from Ben White's delivery. Against a team defending deep and matched man-for-man in a 4-2-3-1, that is often the most reliable door left open.
lesson.spotIt: Next match, count the corners and watch who Arsenal send into the box — if Gabriel and the other centre-backs are jogging forward every time, Arsenal are treating set-pieces as a scoring plan, not a bonus.

statTranslations.plain: Arsenal spent the match pinning Everton in and forcing the ball out for throws and corners — and both goals came from that pressure, scored by two centre-backs.

statTranslations.stat: Touches in opposition box: Arsenal 47 | Everton 17
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal got the ball into the dangerous area almost three times as often, which is territorial control rather than just keeping possession for its own sake.

statTranslations.stat: Total shots 20 v 8, but shots on target 4 v 3
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal created far more volume but didn't test the goalkeeper much more than Everton did — a lot of those 20 attempts were blocked or missed the target.

The chances Arsenal created were worth about two goals before the shots were taken, and slightly more once you saw where those shots ended up — Arsenal's efforts on target were better placed than average.

statTranslations.stat: Tackles: Everton 17 | Arsenal 14, interceptions Everton 8 | Arsenal 4
statTranslations.plain: Everton made more defensive actions not because they pressed harder but because they were the team constantly having to defend.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal went to Munich and traded punches with Bayern. Ødegaard set up Eberechi Eze to put Arsenal ahead on 25 minutes, but Alphonso Davies levelled it on 35 and Harry Kane put Bayern in front on 61. With eight minutes left Declan Rice finished off a Viktor Gyökeres assist to make it 2-2. Arsenal saw more of the ball (54%) and had slightly more shots (14 to 13), but Bayern created the better openings and the draw was a fair reflection of a genuinely even, high-quality night.
explained.opponentPlan: Kompany set Bayern up in a mirror image, 4-2-3-1 against 4-2-3-1, which means every Arsenal player in build-up has a natural opponent standing in front of them — the hardest kind of game to pass your way through. Bayern conceded the ball willingly (46% possession, and only 173 passes in the opposition half to Arsenal's 253) and backed themselves to hurt Arsenal when they won it back, which they did: 29 touches in Arsenal's box against Arsenal's 22, and 10 of their 13 shots from inside the area. Arsenal's answer was to accept the ball and work it patiently — more possession, more corners (5 to 3), more territory — while defending the resulting counter-attacks aggressively, and their 12 interceptions to Bayern's 2 shows a team actively trying to intercept Bayern's forward passes rather than simply absorbing them. It mostly worked, but Bayern still manufactured four big chances to Arsenal's three.
explained.keyMoment: Harry Kane's goal on 61 minutes is the hinge of the match: Arsenal had led from the 25th minute, been pegged back by Davies on 35, and now had to chase for the first time all night. Needing a goal with half an hour left is what pushes a side into taking more risks higher up the pitch — and the reward came through two players who were not in the starting eleven, Gyökeres setting up Rice on 82 for 2-2. The scoreline pattern (lead, level, behind, level) tells you this was a game neither side ever controlled for long.
explained.nerdCorner: The number that should bother you is not xG, it is xGOT: Arsenal 1.68 from 1.69 xG, Bayern 2.18 from 2.46. Arsenal essentially converted the full value of their chances into shots on target — nothing was dragged wide, nothing was wasted, and they still only scored twice from 1.68 xGOT, meaning Neuer's goal did not get beaten by anything lucky. Bayern, by contrast, shed 0.28 of value between the chance and the strike and still produced 2.18 xGOT from four big chances. Put another way: Arsenal needed near-perfect finishing execution to draw, Bayern did not, and Raya's three saves were holding back a materially bigger wave than the three saves at the other end. The other quiet tension here is the mirrored 4-2-3-1. When shapes match man-for-man, the team that wins is usually the one whose full-backs create the extra man — which is exactly why the overlap/underlap question and that stepped-in full-back matter more than the 54% possession figure. Arsenal got the territory (253 passes in Bayern's half) but Bayern got the box (29 touches), and that scissors — lots of the ball, fewer dangerous entries — is the recurring away-leg problem worth tracking across the group.

shape.plainEnglish: A 4-2-3-1 on the teamsheet almost never stays a 4-2-3-1 once Arsenal actually have the ball. Typically one full-back — with Timber and Calafiori as the pair, usually Timber — steps inside next to the two holding midfielders, which leaves three defenders behind the ball and two screeners in front of them, while the wingers stay wide and Havertz and Ødegaard occupy the space between Bayern's defence and midfield. The moment possession is lost, that stepped-in full-back sprints back out to his own side and the team snaps into two banks of four, which is why the same eleven players look like two different teams depending on who has the ball.

lesson.explain: A press is not eleven players deciding independently to run at the ball — it is the whole team going at the same instant because of an agreed cue. That cue is the pressing trigger: a backwards pass, a heavy first touch, a ball played to a defender who is already facing his own goal, or a pass into a player with an opponent tight behind him. Arsenal's 12 interceptions to Bayern's 2 is the fingerprint of this: an interception usually means a defender had already started moving before the pass was played, because the trigger told him it was coming. Bayern, defending in the same 4-2-3-1 shape, were far more content to let Arsenal have the ball and stay compact — hence Arsenal's 253 passes in the opposition half against Bayern's 173, and Bayern's grand total of 2 interceptions.
lesson.spotIt: Watch the Arsenal forward nearest the ball when an opponent plays a square or backwards pass — the second that pass leaves his foot, you will see three or four Arsenal players sprint forward together, not one.

statTranslations.plain: Based on the quality of the chances created, Bayern would be expected to score roughly one more goal than Arsenal on an average night — so 2-2 was a good return from an away trip where Arsenal were second best for openings.
Bayern got into the most dangerous area of the pitch more often than Arsenal did, despite having the ball less — the sign of a team that moves it quickly and directly once it wins possession.
Arsenal spent far more of the night camped in Bayern's half, which is territorial control — but it did not convert into more box entries, which is the gap between dominating and threatening.
Arsenal were reading and cutting out Bayern's passes rather than waiting to tackle; Bayern barely did this at all, because they were set up to stay in shape and let Arsenal come to them.

statTranslations.stat: Shots inside box: 9 vs 10, shots on target 5 vs 5
statTranslations.plain: Almost identical volume and accuracy from both sides — the difference between these teams was the quality of the chances, not the number of them.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal went to Nottingham Forest and had the ball almost all afternoon — 74% of it — but for 80 minutes they couldn't find a way through a packed home defence. Forest actually had more shots (14 to Arsenal's 9), mostly from distance or from set pieces, and forced David Raya into two saves. Then on 80 minutes Declan Rice set up substitute Noni Madueke for the only goal of the game, and Arsenal held on to win 1-0.
explained.keyMoment: The 80th minute. Until then the game had settled into a stalemate that the numbers describe perfectly: Arsenal with 335 passes in the opposition half to Forest's 68, and still only one shot on target to show for it. Declan Rice's assist for Noni Madueke broke it — Arsenal's one big chance of the match (1 to Forest's 0) converted at the only moment it needed to be. Everything before that was the same pattern repeated; the goal is the only thing in the data that changes the picture.
explained.nerdCorner: The gap between xG and xGOT is the most interesting thing in this data set. Arsenal's xG was 1.14 but their xG on target was only 0.19 — meaning that of all the chances they generated, the ones that actually reached Hennessey's goal were worth almost nothing. Forest were the same, 0.9 down to 0.12. That isn't a finishing story so much as a blocking-and-shooting-position story: Arsenal had 7 shots inside the box and got precisely 1 on target, which usually means bodies in the way rather than wayward strikers. A 74% possession, 335-passes-in-their-half performance that produces a single shot on target is a side that controlled where the game was played without ever controlling what happened in the six-yard box — and it was a substitute, Madueke, who finally changed that. Worth holding alongside the corner count, too: Forest had 8 corners to Arsenal's 6 despite 26% of the ball, which is where a lot of those 14 shots will have come from.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper Arsenal line up 4-2-3-1, but a team's shape with the ball and without it are almost never the same thing. With the ball, this Arteta side typically pushes one full-back high and tucks the other in alongside the two deeper midfielders, so the back four becomes a back three, two players sit in front of them to recycle possession, and five attackers spread across the final third — hence 3-2-5. Without the ball it collapses back the other way: Ødegaard steps up next to Havertz, Saka and Eze drop into a line of four, and you get a 4-4-2. The player whose movement does most of the work is the full-back, usually Calafiori or Ben White, whose decision to go high or tuck inside is what turns four defenders into three.

lesson.explain: There are two ways to defend: you either follow a specific opponent wherever he goes (man-marking), or you take responsibility for a patch of grass and deal with whoever enters it (zonal). Glasner's teams lean heavily on the man-oriented version, and the tackle count here is the fingerprint of it — Forest made 22 tackles to Arsenal's 9. That number is high not because Forest were better defenders but because man-marking means you are constantly arriving at an opponent and engaging him, rather than standing in a zone and letting the ball come to you. The trade-off is visible in the other direction too: Arsenal still got 30 touches in the Forest box, because if you man-mark all over the pitch, a single clever movement drags your marker out of the shape and leaves a hole where he was standing.
lesson.spotIt: When an Arsenal player makes a run, watch the defender nearest him rather than the ball — if the defender turns and follows him across the pitch, that's man-marking; if he stays put and hands him over to a teammate, that's zonal.

statTranslations.plain: Arsenal had the ball nearly three times as much, which tells you Forest were content to sit in and let Arsenal come to them rather than contest the game.
Arsenal spent the match camped in Forest's territory — Forest barely got the ball into Arsenal's half at all, let alone kept it there.

statTranslations.stat: Total shots 9 vs 14, shots on target 1 vs 2
statTranslations.plain: Forest had more attempts than Arsenal despite almost never having the ball, which means their shots were coming from quick moments and set pieces rather than sustained attacks — and almost nothing from either side actually tested a goalkeeper.
Across 90 minutes only one genuinely clear scoring opportunity was created in the entire match, and Arsenal took it.
Forest were doing more than twice as much physical defending, which is what happens when one team is defending its own box and the other is passing around in front of it.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal controlled the match from the start but could not find a way through for an hour — Lille defended deep, kept bodies in front of their goal and did not manage a single shot on target all night. Then the game broke open in seven minutes: Timber scored on 64, Eze on 67, and Saka on 71. Lille's goalkeeper made five saves, Raya made none, and the 3-0 scoreline arguably flatters Lille rather than Arsenal.
explained.opponentPlan: Davide Ancelotti set Lille up in a 4-3-3, but the numbers say that was a defensive 4-3-3 — the two wide forwards tucking back to make a compact block and the three midfielders screening in front of the back four. The evidence is in the territory: Lille completed only 86 passes in the opposition half to Arsenal's 319, and registered three touches in Arsenal's box all match. They also made more tackles (19 v 16) and more interceptions (8 v 6) than Arsenal, which is what happens when you spend the night defending your own penalty area rather than contesting the ball up the pitch. Arsenal's answer was to accept the possession (58%), work the ball wide and win corners — seven of them, against Lille's zero — and keep loading the box until the structure cracked.
explained.keyMoment: The seven-minute window between 64' and 71'. Timber's goal from Madueke's assist on 64 was the first crack; Eze made it two on 67 from Saka's pass, and Saka scored the third on 71, assisted by Kai Havertz — two of those three goals involved players who had come off the bench, and the fresh legs arriving into a defence that had been retreating for an hour is the pattern the scoreline is hiding.
explained.nerdCorner: The interesting tension is between the xG (1.7) and the xGOT (1.95). xG measures how good the chances were at the moment of the shot; xGOT measures how good the shots were once struck, counting only efforts on target. When xGOT comes in above xG, it means the finishing and shot placement beat the raw quality of the openings — Arsenal did not just manufacture 16 shots, they hit the corners with them. Pair that with Lille's xGOT of 0.0 and you get the real story: Arsenal over-performed their chance quality and Lille produced literally nothing on target from 0.3 xG. The other thing worth flagging is the tackle and interception count going Lille's way (19-16, 8-6). Beginners read that as 'Lille competed more'. It is the opposite — defensive actions pile up for the team that is permanently defending, and the four big chances to zero tells you who was actually winning the duels that mattered.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper Arsenal line up 4-2-3-1, but a back four and two holding midfielders is not a great way to attack a team sitting deep — you end up with too many players behind the ball and not enough in dangerous areas. So with the ball this side usually slides into something closer to a 3-2-5: one full-back (typically Timber on the right) tucks inside or stays back to make a back three, the other pushes high, and five players occupy the width and the space between the opposition defenders. When possession is lost, those front players drop back into two banks of four and Arsenal defend as a 4-4-2 again. The full-backs' movement is what causes the shape to flip back and forth.

lesson.explain: An inverted full-back is a defender who, instead of running up and down the touchline, steps inside into the middle of the pitch when his team has the ball. The point is control: it puts an extra body in central midfield, which means more short passing options against a packed defence and more cover if possession is lost. Arsenal's 4-2-3-1 typically uses Timber this way on the right — he tucks in alongside Rice and Bruno Guimarães, which frees Madueke to stay wide and lets Lewis-Skelly push high on the left. The reward showed up on the scoresheet: Timber, nominally a full-back, was the one who scored on 64 from Madueke's assist, because an inverted full-back finishes attacks from central areas rather than from the corner flag.
lesson.spotIt: When Arsenal have the ball in the opposition half, ignore the ball and watch the right-back — if he drifts into the middle of the pitch next to Declan Rice instead of running down the wing, you're watching an inverted full-back.

statTranslations.plain: Lille never once forced Raya into a save — this was a one-way game, not a tight one.

statTranslations.stat: Touches in opposition box: Arsenal 54 | Lille 3
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal got the ball into the danger area eighteen times more often than Lille did, which is the single clearest measure of territorial dominance.
Three quarters of Arsenal's shots came from close range rather than hopeful long-range efforts, which is why the quality of chances was so lopsided.
The scoreline could have been bigger — Lille's goalkeeper was the busiest player on the pitch and Arsenal's had nothing to do.
Lille never got close enough to Arsenal's goal to win a single corner, while Arsenal kept forcing the ball into the box until something gave.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal controlled the ball for most of the afternoon and spent far more time camped near the Leeds goal, but the first goal went the other way: James Justin scored for Leeds on 55 minutes after a pass from Gabriel Gudmundsson. Arsenal needed seven minutes to level, Riccardo Calafiori finishing from a Ben White pass on 62. Eight minutes later Declan Rice set up Bruno Guimarães for the winner, and it finished 2-1.
explained.opponentPlan: Daniel Farke set Leeds up in a 3-5-2, which is a shape built to be hard to play through the middle: three centre-backs, three central midfielders, and two strikers who can stay high rather than tracking back. The trade-off is width — a 3-5-2 has only two wing-backs covering both touchlines, so if Arsenal get the ball to the far side quickly, someone has to sprint 50 yards to meet it. Arsenal's 58% possession and 266 passes in the opposition half against Leeds' 105 show which way that balance tipped: Arsenal were allowed the ball and used it to keep stretching that five-man midfield line sideways, ending with 37 touches in the Leeds box to Leeds' 17. What Leeds did get from the setup was danger on the break and from set pieces — two strikers already high up the pitch meant every turnover was a threat, and they won four corners to Arsenal's two.
explained.keyMoment: The 55th minute, when James Justin put Leeds ahead against the run of play from a Gabriel Gudmundsson assist. Up to that point Arsenal had been accumulating territory without a breakthrough; going behind forced them to attack a Leeds side that could now legitimately sit deeper and defend its lead. The answer came from the widest parts of the pitch — Ben White found Calafiori for 2-1... sorry, for 1-1 on 62, and Rice found Bruno Guimarães on 70 for the winner. Two goals in eight minutes, both created by players who start the game nominally behind the forward line.
explained.nerdCorner: The interesting split here is xG 2.33 vs 0.62 against xGOT 2.11 vs 1.83. Leeds' xGOT being nearly three times their xG means their shots on target were struck far better than the positions they came from deserved — that is finishing and shot placement, which is the least repeatable thing in football, not a structural weakness in Arsenal's defending. Arsenal's own xGOT (2.11) sitting slightly below their xG (2.33) is the more normal picture. The other thing worth noting is that the shot volumes were nearly level (13-11, six on target to five, eight inside the box to seven) while the territorial numbers were lopsided (37 box touches to 17, 266 passes in the opposition half to 105). That combination — control of territory but not of shot count — is the price of playing against a 3-5-2 with two strikers permanently high: Leeds' chances came from a small number of moments rather than sustained pressure, and four corners to Arsenal's two gave them a route to goal that doesn't require possession at all.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper Arsenal line up 4-2-3-1, but a back four and two midfielders is a defensive arrangement, not an attacking one. With the ball this group usually rearranges itself: one full-back steps inside next to Declan Rice to form a two-man base, the other full-back and the centre-backs make a back three behind them, and five players spread across the width of the final third. That full-back stepping inside is the movement that does it — he vacates the touchline so Saka or Madueke can stay wide and isolated against a defender, and he adds a body in central midfield so Arsenal can keep circulating the ball. When possession is lost the full-back simply drops back out to his side and the familiar flat four reappears.

lesson.explain: A switch is a long diagonal pass that takes the ball from one touchline to the other in a single move. It matters because defending is a sideways-shuffling job: when Leeds' 3-5-2 slides across to crowd the ball, the far side is left with one wing-back covering a huge amount of grass, and a ball that travels 50 yards in two seconds arrives faster than a defender can run it. That is the structural reason Arsenal's full-backs end up so involved in the final third — Ben White assisting Calafiori is the signature of a team working the ball side to side until a wide player is free near the box. The numbers underneath it are the 266 passes in the Leeds half against 105, and 37 touches in the opposition box against 17: Arsenal weren't just passing more, they were passing in the areas where a switch actually pays off.
lesson.spotIt: Watch the far-side Arsenal full-back or winger rather than the ball — if he is standing alone on the opposite touchline with no one near him, a switch is coming, and the whole Leeds defence will have to sprint sideways to reach him.

statTranslations.plain: Arsenal built up more than three times the quality of chance Leeds did — the 2-1 scoreline flatters Leeds considerably.
Leeds' shots were far better placed than they were created — they turned 0.62 worth of chances into 1.83 worth of finishing, which is the kind of shooting you cannot rely on repeating.
Arsenal didn't just have the ball, they had it in the one area that actually produces goals, more than twice as often.
Leeds spent the match defending their own territory; Arsenal essentially played the game in Leeds' half.

statTranslations.stat: Total shots 13 vs 11, big chances 4 vs 2
statTranslations.plain: The shot counts look close, but Arsenal's were the better ones — raw shot totals hide chance quality, which is exactly what big chances and xG are for.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal had the ball for most of this game — 60% of it — and spent long spells camped in Brighton's half, but they lost 3-0. Brighton scored through Pascal Groß on 31 minutes, added a second right on 45 minutes through Charalampos Kostoulas, and killed it off when Chema Andrés made it three on 57. Brighton had fewer of the ball but more shots (17 to 11) and more shots on target (5 to 2), and every time they got a clean sight of goal they hit it properly.
explained.opponentPlan: Brighton set up in a mirror 4-2-3-1 under Fabian Hürzeler and were plainly content to let Arsenal have the ball — 40% possession and only 135 passes in the opposition half says they weren't chasing territory. Their work was done further back and higher up in bursts: 19 tackles and 11 interceptions to Arsenal's 13 and 6 means Brighton were the team actively winning the ball off someone, not the team calmly recycling it. Arsenal's answer was volume — 196 passes in Brighton's half, 36 touches in their box, 6 corners — but Arsenal's 4-2-3-1 pushes so many bodies forward that each Brighton ball-win started a race Arsenal were behind in, and Brighton finished with 17 shots to Arsenal's 11.
explained.keyMoment: The 45th minute. Arsenal had been chasing the game since Groß scored on 31, and going in at half-time one down with all their possession is a manageable problem. Kostoulas making it 2-0 right on 45, assisted by Diego Gómez, turned it into a different match: Arsenal now had to commit even more bodies forward, which is exactly the situation Brighton had been feeding on, and Chema Andrés's third on 57 — assisted by Groß, the man who scored the first — came from the same pattern.
explained.nerdCorner: The scoreline hides that this was, by expected goals, a near-even match: 1.63 to 1.31, with Arsenal even edging touches in the opposition box 36-30. The gap opens up entirely at the point of contact. Arsenal's xG of 1.63 became an xGOT of 1.08 — the shots they took were worth less once struck than they were when the chance appeared. Brighton's 1.31 became 2.04, a full chance better. Add that both teams had exactly 10 shots inside the box, and you have a match where the locations were comparable and the executions were not. The harder question is whether that's noise or structure: Arsenal's 11 shots for 36 box touches suggests a lot of entering the area and not much finishing the move, which is a pattern rather than a coin flip, while Brighton's 5 shots on target from 17 attempts producing three goals is the kind of conversion rate that does not repeat. Both things can be true — Arsenal were unlucky on the day and still had a real problem converting territory into clean shots.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper Arsenal line up 4-2-3-1, but a team with Timber and Calafiori as full-backs and Rice plus Bruno Guimarães behind Ødegaard usually doesn't stay in neat rows once they have the ball. Typically one full-back tucks inside next to the deeper midfielders while the other pushes high, which leaves three defenders across the back, two in front of them and five players spread along the last line. Without the ball those same players have to sprint back out to the touchlines and reform two banks of four, and that journey — inside to outside, high to deep — is where a team is at its most stretched.

lesson.explain: Rest defence is the group of players you deliberately keep back while your own attack is happening — the insurance policy for the moment you lose the ball. It matters most to exactly this kind of team: Arsenal had 60% of the ball and 196 passes in Brighton's half, meaning for most of 90 minutes their defenders were high up the pitch with a lot of grass behind them. Brighton made 19 tackles and 11 interceptions, so they were repeatedly taking the ball off Arsenal in those moments, and they ended up with 17 shots to Arsenal's 11 despite seeing far less of the ball. When the team with 40% possession out-shoots you by six, the question is rarely about your attack — it's about who was standing where when your attack broke down.
lesson.spotIt: Next match, when Arsenal have the ball near the opposition box, ignore the ball for five seconds and count how many Arsenal players are still behind it — that number is the rest defence, and watch what happens to it the moment possession is lost.

statTranslations.plain: Having the ball is not the same as having chances — Brighton did more damage with less of it.
xGOT measures the quality of shots once they're struck; Brighton's finishing upgraded their chances, Arsenal's downgraded theirs.
The underlying chance quality was close to level — this was not a 3-0 performance gap, it was a 3-0 finishing gap.
Brighton were the team actively stealing the ball, and each steal is the starting whistle for a counter.

statTranslations.stat: Touches in opposition box 36 vs 30, shots on target 2 vs 5
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal got into the dangerous area plenty but rarely turned it into a proper test of the goalkeeper.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal went away to Ipswich in the EFL Cup and settled it early: Max Dowman scored in the 7th minute, Noni Madueke added a second on 16, and by the time Dowman got his second just after half-time (47) and Mikel Merino made it four on 58, the tie was effectively over. Ipswich then got two back — Anis Mehmeti on 62 and Chuba Akpom in the 90th minute — which made the final score 4-2 look far tighter than the game felt. Arsenal had more of the ball (59%), more shots (12 to 8), and four big chances to Ipswich's one.
explained.opponentPlan: Ipswich set up in a mirror 4-2-3-1 under Gary O'Neil, which usually means they wanted man-for-man reference points all over the pitch rather than ceding territory. The tackle and interception counts tell you how that went: Ipswich made 26 tackles and 14 interceptions to Arsenal's 17 and 9, the profile of a side constantly reacting to the ball rather than dictating where it goes. Arsenal answered by simply playing through and around them — 286 passes in the opposition half against Ipswich's 158, and 29 touches in the Ipswich box against 19. Once Arsenal led 2-0 inside 16 minutes, Ipswich had to come out and chase, which is exactly the situation their two late goals came from.
explained.keyMoment: The 47th minute. Arsenal came out after the break and Martín Zubimendi — one of the deepest players on the pitch — set up Dowman for 3-0 within two minutes of the restart. That's the moment the tie stopped being competitive: Ipswich had a whole half-time to reset and were behind by three before they'd touched the ball properly. Merino's fourth on 58 followed, and Ipswich's goals on 62 and 90 came only after the game state had already been decided.
explained.nerdCorner: The gap between xG (0.95) and xGOT (2.86) is the whole story of this match and it's the thing to be careful about. xG asks 'how good was the chance?' — and by that measure Arsenal's four goals came from a set of chances worth under one goal. xGOT asks 'how good was the shot?' and Arsenal's 2.86 says the finishing was elite. That's a 1.91 overperformance, and finishing at that level is the least repeatable thing in football. The sustainable, repeatable evidence is elsewhere: 4 big chances to 1, 286 passes in the opposition half to 158, 29 box touches to 19. Those are process numbers and they'd survive a rematch. The 4-2 might not. Equally worth noting the flip side — Ipswich's own xGOT (1.62) sat well above their xG (0.72), and Kepa made just one save all match. Ipswich scored twice from a game in which they created one big chance. A digest that only reads the scoreline concludes 'Arsenal leaky at the back'; a digest that reads xGOT concludes 'two very good finishes against a defence that conceded almost nothing of substance.' Both goals also arrived at 4-0 and in the 90th minute, when game state had removed any reason for Arsenal to hold shape.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper Arsenal lined up 4-2-3-1, but a team's shape with the ball is almost never the shape on the teamsheet. With a young full-back like Myles Lewis-Skelly, Arsenal typically push him forward or tuck him inside so the back four becomes a back three, the two holders (Zubimendi and Bruno Guimarães here) sit in front of it, and five attackers spread across the final third. Without the ball those players sprint back into recognisable banks again, which is why the same eleven can look like two completely different teams depending on who has possession.

lesson.explain: A progressive pass or carry is any time you move the ball meaningfully closer to the opponent's goal — not a sideways reset, but a genuine gain of ground. The single clearest evidence of it in this match is the passing map: Arsenal played 286 passes in the opposition half to Ipswich's 158, and turned that into 29 touches in the Ipswich box against 19. That gap doesn't come from possession alone — 59% isn't overwhelming — it comes from what Arsenal did with the ball once they had it. Zubimendi's assist for the 47th-minute goal is the idea in one action: a deep midfielder whose job is not just to keep the ball but to move it forward into a scoring position.
lesson.spotIt: Next match, pick one Arsenal midfielder and count how many of his passes go forward past an opponent versus sideways to a teammate on the same line — the ratio tells you whether Arsenal are actually progressing or just circulating.

statTranslations.stat: Passes in opposition half: Arsenal 286 | Ipswich 158
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal spent the game camped in Ipswich's half, so almost all of their passing happened in dangerous territory rather than safely in front of their own defence.
Arsenal created four clear openings to Ipswich's one — the scoreline of 4-2 flatters Ipswich considerably.

xG says both teams' chances were fairly ordinary; xGOT measures the quality of the shot once it left the foot, and Arsenal's leap from 0.95 to 2.86 means the finishing was outstanding, not that the chances were.

statTranslations.stat: Tackles: Arsenal 17 | Ipswich 26, Interceptions: Arsenal 9 | Ipswich 14
statTranslations.plain: Ipswich were doing far more defensive work, which is what happens when the other team has the ball and is moving it forward — those are numbers of a side chasing, not controlling.

statTranslations.stat: Shots inside box: Arsenal 9 of 12 | Ipswich 6 of 8
statTranslations.plain: Three quarters of Arsenal's shots came from inside the penalty area, meaning they were working the ball into good positions rather than shooting from distance out of frustration.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal went to Sunderland and won 2-0, but the game was far tighter than the scoreline suggests. Sunderland had more shots (12 to 11) and more touches in the Arsenal box (26 to 19), so Arsenal were genuinely having to defend. The breakthrough came on 58 minutes through Bruno Guimarães, set up by Declan Rice, and Bukayo Saka added a second right at the end on 90 minutes to make the result look comfortable.
explained.opponentPlan: Régis Le Bris set Sunderland up in the same 4-2-3-1 as Arsenal, which is a mirror match: every Arsenal player has a natural opposite number, so nobody is automatically free and the game becomes about who moves first. Sunderland were happy to let Arsenal have the ball — 57% possession to 43% — and instead looked to attack in fast bursts, which is why they managed 12 shots and 26 touches in Arsenal's box despite seeing less of the ball. Arsenal's answer was to dominate the areas in front of that: 169 passes in the opposition half against Sunderland's 108, plus 8 interceptions to 5, which is a side trying to keep the game pinned at the far end and cut passes out early rather than defend a series of raids. It half-worked: Arsenal controlled the territory but never fully smothered Sunderland's counters.
explained.keyMoment: The 58th minute. In a game that had been dead level on chances, Declan Rice fed Bruno Guimarães for the opener — the first goal in a match where both sides had created three big chances each. Once Arsenal led, the pattern was set: Sunderland had to come further forward, which explains how they finished with more shots and more box touches than Arsenal, and it also opened the door for Saka's second on 90 minutes to close it out.
explained.nerdCorner: The scoreline is the least honest number on the page. Arsenal 1.88 xG to Sunderland 1.80, xGOT 1.91 to 1.66, three big chances each — by every underlying measure this was a coin-flip, and a 2-0 away win banks three points that the performance only half-earned. The detail worth chewing on is the split between territory and penetration: Arsenal won the passes-in-the-opposition-half count 169-108 yet lost touches-in-the-box 19-26. That combination — lots of possession high up, fewer entries into the danger area than the opponent — is the classic signature of a side that controls where the game is played without controlling what happens when it gets there, and Sunderland's four corners to Arsenal's two points the same way. Also note Sunderland's xGOT (1.66) sitting below their xG (1.80): their shooting was, on balance, slightly worse than the positions they got into deserved, which is not something you can rely on happening every week.

shape.plainEnglish: The 4-2-3-1 written on the teamsheet is only the starting arrangement — it changes the moment Arsenal have the ball. With this personnel Arsenal usually push both wide forwards high and wide, one full-back tucks inside next to the two midfielders, and the back line becomes a three, which is why you end up with five attackers across the front and a solid five behind them. Myles Lewis-Skelly's movement inside from left-back is typically the one that causes it: he steps into midfield rather than overlapping, which frees Declan Rice to move higher and leaves Gabriel, Ezri Konsa and Ben White covering the back. Without the ball everyone slides back out into recognisable banks of four.

lesson.explain: A formation is just the starting positions written back-to-front, defenders first: 4-2-3-1 means four defenders, two holding midfielders, three attacking midfielders, one striker. Arsenal and Sunderland both lined up 4-2-3-1 here, which tells you something useful straight away — every player had a direct opposite number, so neither side got a free man just from the shape. That's part of why the chance count came out level at three big chances each and the shot counts were 11 to 12. The important thing to understand is that a formation is a starting point, not a cage: the numbers on the teamsheet describe where players stand before kick-off, and the moment the ball moves, so do they.
lesson.spotIt: At kick-off, count the back line, then the players just in front of them, then work forward — that's the formation, and then watch how quickly it stops looking like that once Arsenal have the ball for ten seconds.

statTranslations.stat: Possession 57% vs 43%, passes in opposition half 169 vs 108
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal held the ball and held it in the right half of the pitch — Sunderland were playing a lot of the game in their own territory.

statTranslations.stat: Touches in opposition box: Arsenal 19, Sunderland 26
statTranslations.plain: Sunderland actually got into Arsenal's penalty area more often, so the 2-0 hides how much defending Arsenal had to do.

statTranslations.stat: Total shots 11 vs 12, big chances 3 vs 3
statTranslations.plain: On raw chance creation this was an even match — Arsenal won it on finishing and timing, not on volume.
Arsenal made their attempts count more often, forcing the keeper into work while Sunderland's efforts more often missed the target entirely.
Arsenal were reading passes and stepping in front of them rather than waiting to make last-ditch tackles.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal went to Napoli, took control of the ball and spent most of the night camped in Napoli's half, but couldn't find a way through for over an hour. Napoli barely attacked at all — five shots all match, no corners — and relied on their goalkeeper, who made six saves. Martin Ødegaard finally settled it on 75 minutes, finishing an assist from Christos Tzolis, and it ended 1-0 to Arsenal.
explained.opponentPlan: Napoli matched Arsenal's 4-2-3-1 on paper but played it very differently: Allegri's side conceded the ball (42% possession) and defended deep and compact, accepting territory in exchange for keeping bodies between Arsenal and their goal. The numbers show it clearly — Napoli made 14 tackles to Arsenal's 9 and had only 126 passes in the opposition half, so they were defending and clearing rather than building. Arsenal's answer was volume and width: 433 passes in Napoli's half, 51 touches in the box and 26 shots, working the ball side to side until a gap appeared, while Napoli's total lack of a counter-attacking threat (0 big chances) meant Arsenal could keep committing bodies forward without much risk.
explained.keyMoment: The 75th minute, Ødegaard's goal from a Christos Tzolis assist. Until then the pattern was total Arsenal control with no reward — 26 shots and 6 saves from the Napoli goalkeeper tell you how long the door stayed shut. The goal didn't change the shape of the game so much as finally cash in the shape of the game that had existed since kick-off, and it came from a captain arriving in the box rather than from the wide players who had been doing most of the crossing.
explained.nerdCorner: The gap between xG 4.05 and xGOT 1.69 is the real story, and it's a different story from the one the scoreline tells. xG asks "how good was the opening?"; xGOT asks "how good was the shot once it left the boot?" — it only counts efforts that reached the goal. So Arsenal generated four goals' worth of openings and delivered under two goals' worth of on-target attempts, with 26 shots but only 8 on target. That is a finishing/shot-selection shortfall, not a chance-creation shortfall, and it's the more encouraging of the two problems to have: chance creation is a repeatable team process, whereas conversion at this volume regresses toward the mean fairly quickly. The flip side of the trade-off: sustaining 433 passes in the opposition half against a side that offers nothing on the break (0 big chances, 5 shots) is comparatively cheap. The interesting question is whether the same shape holds up against an opponent who actually punishes a high, committed back line.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper Arsenal lined up 4-2-3-1, but a back four with the ball usually becomes a back three: one full-back (typically Ben White on the right) tucks in alongside the centre-backs while Piero Hincapié pushes high up the left touchline. That leaves two holding midfielders — Declan Rice and Mikel Merino — screening in front, and five players spread across the last line to stretch the opponent's defence as wide as possible. When Arsenal lose the ball, Hincapié drops back in and the wide attackers fall into a flat line, so the shape reverts to two banks of four with Viktor Gyökeres and Martin Ødegaard nearest the ball.

lesson.explain: Picture the pitch cut into five vertical lanes: two touchlines, the central lane, and the two lanes in between — those in-between lanes are the half-spaces. They matter because a defender standing there doesn't know whether he belongs to the centre-back or the full-back, so a runner arriving in that lane is often nobody's problem until it's too late. That is exactly the territory a No. 10 like Ødegaard lives in, and it's why 51 touches in Napoli's box came from a team facing a deep, compact defence: when the middle is packed and the touchlines are covered, the half-space is the only lane left to attack. His 75th-minute finish is the archetype — the ball goes wide to Tzolis, the defence shifts toward the touchline, and the goal comes from someone arriving between the lines rather than from a straight run through the centre.
lesson.spotIt: Watch Ødegaard when Saka has the ball on the right touchline — he'll drift into the gap between Napoli's right-back and their nearest centre-back, and that patch of grass is the half-space.

statTranslations.plain: From the quality of chances created, a typical night with this pattern of play ends with Arsenal scoring around four and Napoli scoring nothing — so 1-0 flatters Napoli enormously.

The chances were worth roughly four goals, but the shots that actually reached the goalkeeper were only worth about 1.7 — meaning a lot of good openings were skewed wide or blocked rather than being saved.
Arsenal created five clear openings and Napoli created literally none — this was not a game that could plausibly have gone the other way.

statTranslations.stat: Shots inside box 15 vs 2, touches in opposition box 51 vs 8
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal weren't just having more of the ball, they were having it in the most dangerous 18 yards of the pitch, which is the difference between sterile possession and genuine pressure.
Napoli's night was pure containment — their keeper was their most active attacking-phase contributor and they never once forced Arsenal to defend a set piece.

explained.whatHappened: Chelsea scored almost immediately — Morgan Rogers finished a Jorrel Hato pass in the 2nd minute — and Arsenal spent the rest of the match chasing the game they were already better in. Kai Havertz levelled it on 25 minutes from a Declan Rice pass, and five minutes into the second half Martin Ødegaard put Arsenal ahead after Christos Tzolis set him up. Arsenal had 16 shots to Chelsea's 13, but 13 of Arsenal's came from inside the box, and Chelsea's goalkeeper had to make 8 saves to keep the score that close.
explained.opponentPlan: Xabi Alonso's 3-4-2-1 is built to be hard to play through — three centre-backs, a flat four in midfield, and two forwards tucked just behind the striker — and it gives you an extra man at the back to defend against Arsenal's five-across-the-front. Chelsea got their reward inside two minutes through Rogers, then had a lead to protect, and the numbers show what that turned into: Arsenal 54% possession, 267 passes in the opposition half to Chelsea's 191, and 44 touches in the Chelsea box against 26. Arsenal's answer was not to force it through the middle of those three centre-backs but to keep arriving in the box from wide and from the second line — 13 of their 16 shots came from inside the area, and Chelsea created zero big chances all match against Arsenal's four.
explained.keyMoment: Ødegaard's goal on 50 minutes, assisted by Tzolis. Arsenal had already equalised through Havertz on 25 and had spent the rest of the first half with the ball; scoring so soon after the restart meant Chelsea, who had been defending a lead in a five-at-the-back shape, now had to come out and chase. From there Arsenal never conceded another big chance — Chelsea finished the match with zero — while Chelsea's keeper ended up making 8 saves.
explained.nerdCorner: The scoreline hides how lopsided the chance quality was: Arsenal's xG on target was 2.0 against a total xG of 2.05, meaning almost everything they generated actually forced a save rather than being blocked or dragged wide — that is unusually clean finishing volume, and it's why the Chelsea keeper's save count reached 8. Chelsea's profile is the mirror image: 13 shots but only 5 inside the box, 0.39 xG and zero big chances, which is the signature of a team that has a lead, sits in a back five, and takes what it can get from range. Note too that Chelsea won the tackle count 12-10 while Arsenal won interceptions 9-7 — tackles are what you make when the ball is already being carried at you, interceptions are what you make when you've read the pass, and that small split is consistent with Chelsea defending their own third while Arsenal squeezed the game higher up (267 passes in the opposition half to 191).

shape.plainEnglish: On paper Arsenal lined up 4-2-3-1, but a back four with Riccardo Calafiori at left-back rarely stays a flat four when Arsenal have the ball. Calafiori typically steps forward or inside while Ben White tucks in alongside Ezri Konsa and Gabriel, which leaves three defenders at the back, two holders in Declan Rice and Myles Lewis-Skelly in front of them, and five attackers across the last line — Saka, Ødegaard, Havertz, Tzolis and whoever pushes up from full-back. When Arsenal lose the ball those five drop back into two banks of four with two players nearest the ball, which is what people mean by a 4-4-2 mid block.

lesson.explain: A transition is the five or ten seconds right after the ball changes hands, before either team is organised again — and it is when most goals are scored, because defenders are out of position. Chelsea's goal on 2 minutes is the purest example: that early in a match nobody has settled, Hato found Rogers, and it was 1-0 before Arsenal's shape existed. The rest of the match shows the flip side — once both teams were set, Chelsea managed 13 shots but only 5 from inside the box and zero big chances, because chances against an organised defence come from further out and at worse angles. Arsenal's two goals, from Rice to Havertz and Tzolis to Ødegaard, came from a team that had the ball 54% of the time and kept walking into the box: 44 touches in there, 13 shots from inside it.
lesson.spotIt: The instant Arsenal lose the ball, count to five and watch how many red shirts are sprinting back rather than towards the ball — that count tells you whether Arsenal are trying to win the transition or survive it.

statTranslations.plain: Chelsea never once got into a genuinely good scoring position after the second minute — their goal came from the one moment nobody was organised.
Both teams shot a similar number of times overall, but Arsenal were shooting from good places and Chelsea mostly weren't.
The quality of chances says this should have been roughly a two-goal Arsenal win, which is exactly what happened — the 2-1 is not a fluke.
Chelsea's keeper had twice as much work to do, which is usually the clearest sign of who spent the match under pressure.

statTranslations.stat: Touches in opposition box: Arsenal 44 | Chelsea 26
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal got into the dangerous area far more often, not just once or twice in a lucky spell.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal had the ball for most of the afternoon at Villa Park and spent the first hour probing without breaking through. Bukayo Saka finally scored on 59 minutes, set up by Riccardo Calafiori. Villa had as many shots as Arsenal — seven each — but not one of them hit the target, and David Raya finished the game without making a single save.
explained.opponentPlan: Villa lined up in the same 4-2-3-1 as Arsenal, which means every Arsenal player had a natural opponent in front of them — a mirror match. Unai Emery's side conceded the ball willingly (39% possession) and defended by making contact: 20 tackles to Arsenal's 13, but only 2 interceptions to Arsenal's 8. That is the profile of a team reacting to the ball rather than reading passes ahead of time. Arsenal's answer was volume and patience in Villa's half — 237 passes there against Villa's 147, and 21 touches in the opposition box — pushing Villa deeper and deeper until a gap opened on the hour.
explained.keyMoment: The 59th minute: Calafiori to Saka, 1-0. In a mirrored 4-2-3-1 the game had been stuck for an hour — every Arsenal player marked by his opposite number — and the breakthrough came from the one player whose starting position doesn't match anyone's: the left-back arriving high on the far side of the pitch to feed the right winger. Everything after it was game management, and Villa's response amounted to zero shots on target all match.
explained.nerdCorner: The scoreline says 1-0 and the shot count says 7-7, but the honest number is xGOT 0.8 to 0.0. Villa managed seven attempts and did not put one on target — Raya recorded zero saves. That is not luck; it is what happens when a team has to shoot from wherever the ball squirts loose rather than from positions they built. The interception split (8-2) is the tell underneath it: Arsenal were intercepting passes, which means they were positioned in the passing lanes before the ball moved, while Villa's 20 tackles show a defence arriving after the fact. A tackle-heavy, interception-light profile is usually a team that is reacting rather than anticipating — it keeps you in a game, but it hands the opponent the tempo. On these numbers, 1-0 flatters Villa more than it flatters Arsenal.

shape.plainEnglish: A 4-2-3-1 is just the starting positions; it is not where players stand once the ball is moving. With this personnel Arsenal usually slide one full-back inside or push the other high, so the back four becomes a back three with two midfielders screening in front — and five attackers spread across the last line. Calafiori is typically the player who causes that shift, stepping infield or advancing from left-back, which is exactly the kind of position from which a left-back ends up creating a goal.

lesson.explain: An overload just means getting more players into one area of the pitch than the opponent has defending it. Villa played the same 4-2-3-1 as Arsenal, so on paper every man was matched — and that is precisely why the game was goalless for an hour. The way you break a mirror match is to add a body from somewhere the opponent isn't counting: Arsenal's 237 passes in Villa's half were the process of shifting Villa across and pulling an extra player into one zone, and the goal on 59 minutes came with Calafiori — a defender, not a forward — supplying the pass. That is a numerical advantage created not by having better players in a spot, but by having one more.
lesson.spotIt: When Arsenal have the ball near a touchline, pause and count Arsenal shirts versus opponent shirts in that corner of the screen — if Arsenal have one more, watch how quickly the ball gets played into the box from there.

statTranslations.plain: Villa shot as often as Arsenal but never once forced Raya to make a save, so the equal shot count is misleading — the quality gap was total.
Arsenal created two genuinely good openings and Villa created none; the chances Villa did take were the difficult, hopeful kind.
Once you only count shots that actually hit the goal, Villa's attacking output rounds to literally nothing.
Arsenal defended by reading and stepping in front of passes; Villa defended by chasing and lunging after the pass had already arrived.

statTranslations.stat: Passes in the opposition half 237 vs 147
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal spent the game camped in Villa territory, which is why Villa's seven shots never came from good positions.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal took control early and never gave it back: Kai Havertz scored on 15 minutes from a Riccardo Calafiori pass, and Bukayo Saka made it two on 23. Four minutes into the second half Martin Ødegaard added a third, set up by Ben White. Arsenal had 20 shots to Coventry's 4 and kept a clean sheet, with David Raya making just one save all afternoon.
explained.opponentPlan: Coventry set up in a matching 4-3-3, which on paper means every Arsenal player has a direct opponent, but they spent the game defending rather than pressing: 36% possession, only 159 passes in the opposition half to Arsenal's 335, and just 3 touches in the Arsenal box all match. Their 9 interceptions against Arsenal's 5 tells you they were sitting off, reading passing lanes and trying to spring forward rather than hunting the ball. Arsenal's answer was simply to keep the ball moving and stretch that back line — 8 corners, 10 shots from inside the box, and 36 touches in Coventry's penalty area meant Lampard's side were pinned in and never got the platform to counter.
explained.keyMoment: The 23rd minute. Havertz's opener on 15 already forced Coventry to chase the game, but Saka's second eight minutes later removed any incentive for them to come out, and the pattern was fixed for the next 70 minutes. Ødegaard's goal on 49 — assisted by Ben White, a full-back — was the same pattern simply repeating after the break.
explained.nerdCorner: Look at the one line that refuses to fit the story: big chances, 1 apiece. Coventry created exactly as many clear openings as Arsenal did, off 4 shots and 3 box touches — a wildly efficient use of their few moments forward. Arsenal's 1.88 xG was assembled from volume, not a single knockout opportunity: 20 shots, 8 corners, 36 box touches, and a 1 goalkeeper save total for Raya that flatters the defensive work as much as it describes it. The gap between xG 1.88 and xGOT 2.44 says the finishing outperformed the chances by a meaningful margin, which is the sort of thing that regresses. The process here — pinning a matching 4-3-3 in its own third and refusing to let it out — is far more repeatable than the conversion rate that turned it into 3-0.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper both teams lined up 4-3-3, but a team's shape on the teamsheet is only the shape they defend in. With the ball, an Arteta side like this usually slides one full-back inside next to the holding midfielder and pushes the other high, so the back four becomes a back three, two players screen in front of it, and five attackers spread across the last line. The movement of the full-backs — Calafiori and White here — is what turns one shape into the other, which is why a defender ends up credited with an assist.

lesson.explain: Both teams were recorded as 4-3-3, yet the game looked nothing like a mirror match — because 4-3-3 only describes how you defend. With the ball, this Arsenal side rearranges: a full-back tucks into midfield, the other pushes high, and the back four effectively becomes a back three feeding five attackers along the last line. That is why Calafiori and Ben White — both defenders on the teamsheet — are the two names credited with assists here, for Havertz on 15 and Ødegaard on 49. A defender producing the final pass is not a fluke; it is the shape doing what it is designed to do.

statTranslations.plain: Arsenal had the ball roughly two minutes in every three, so the shape you were watching for most of the afternoon was the in-possession one, not the 4-3-3.
Arsenal did more than twice as much of their passing inside Coventry's half, meaning the game was played almost entirely in one direction.
Arsenal got into the danger area a dozen times for every one time Coventry did — the clearest single measure of territorial control.
Arsenal's shots were worth roughly 1.88 goals by quality alone, but 2.44 once you account for where they were placed — the finishing was better than the chances.

statTranslations.stat: Shots 20 vs 4, shots inside box 10 vs 1
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal shot five times as often, and half their attempts came from inside the box, which is where shots actually get converted.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal scored after 23 seconds and never trailed. What the scoreline hides is that City had more of the ball, more shots and more touches in Arsenal's box — Arsenal won by creating four clear chances to City's one and putting them away.

shape.plainEnglish: Arsenal started 4-3-3 and City 4-2-3-1, but neither held that shape for long. With the ball Arsenal's left-back steps inside, which turns the back four into a back three and pushes five players onto the last line. Without the ball — which was most of this match — Arsenal folded into two compact banks of four and let City pass in front of them.

explained.opponentPlan: Maresca's City did what they were set up to do: 59% of the ball and 310 passes in Arsenal's half, against Arsenal's 110 in theirs. They got 34 touches in the Arsenal box to Arsenal's 27. What they could not do was turn any of that into a clear opening — one big chance all afternoon, and an xGOT of 0.34 says the few shots they did work were struck straight at Raya.
explained.keyMoment: The first goal, 23 seconds in. Lewis-Skelly found Calafiori for a finish before City had touched the ball. That one moment set the terms for everything after it: Arsenal could sit deep and defend a lead, and City had to come out, which is exactly the game Arsenal wanted.

lesson.explain: This is the match to learn it from, because the stats look like Arsenal lost. City had 59% of the ball, 12 shots to 9, and 34 touches in the box to 27. Arsenal deliberately gave all of that away: they dropped into two banks of four, defended the space in front of their own goal rather than chasing the ball, and made 16 tackles and 10 interceptions doing it. A low block concedes territory on purpose and bets that the opponent will never get a clean look at goal. City managed one big chance. Arsenal managed four.
lesson.spotIt: Next match, when Arsenal are ahead and the opponent has the ball, stop watching the ball and look at the shape. Two flat rows of four, squeezed into the width of the penalty area, with nobody chasing out to press — that is the low block doing its job, and it is not the same thing as being under pressure.

statTranslations.plain: The number that actually explains a 3-0. Arsenal made four genuinely clear openings; City made one.
Arsenal's chances were worth about 2.2 goals and City's about 1.1 — a real edge, but much closer than 3-0 suggests.
Where the match was won. Arsenal struck their shots far better than the chances deserved; City struck theirs far worse, firing straight at Raya.
Arsenal had well under half the ball and were entirely content with that.

statTranslations.stat: Passes in the opposition half: 110 vs 310
statTranslations.plain: City spent almost three times as much of the match camped in Arsenal's territory — and still lost 3-0.

explained.nerdCorner: The xG-to-xGOT gap is the whole story and it cuts both ways. Arsenal turned 2.16 xG into 2.53 xGOT — their finishing beat the quality of the chances. City turned 1.12 into 0.34, meaning their shooting was dreadful relative to the openings. That combined swing is worth roughly two and a half goals of finishing, and it is the least repeatable thing in football: expect both numbers to drift back toward their xG over a season. The more durable read is the big-chance count. Conceding 59% possession and 310 opposition-half passes while allowing exactly one clear sight of goal is a defensive structure working precisely as designed, and that part does repeat.
